extracted.intended_audience: researchers of peer review and science policy, journal editors, reviewers, and methodological critics of academic publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and methodological critique of empirical research on the journal peer-review process, plus recommendations for improving peer review (e.g., blind review, editorial accountability). Targeted at scholars, editors, and reviewers assessing peer-review reliability, bias, and ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to test and control for a variety of possible factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors acknowledge commentators' critique that resubmitting only papers published by authors from high-status institutions limits the ability to rule out alternative interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend a 'grand design' testing many factors simultaneously: Author status (high vs. low) X author institution (prestigious, nonprestigious but real, fictitious) X reviewer status (high vs. low) X reviewer institution (high vs. low) X journal type (blind vs. nonblind) X journal status (high vs. low) X scientific discipline (social vs. physical science) X paper's history (published, rejected, new). One could also add race and sex for affirmative-action–related analyses. Note that such a multifactorial design may require cooperation from journal editors and be infeasible without it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of quasi-experimental designs when full control is impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: When working outside the laboratory, it may be necessary to settle for quasi-experimental approaches that do not rule out all alternative explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quasi-experimental designs can provide causal inferences when used along with convergent evidence, cogent reasoning, valid measurement of threats, and statistical analyses demonstrating threats are not operating (Cook & Campbell 1979).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confounding factor — negative halo effect from suspicious affiliations
rubrics_metrics.description: Using nonacademic or 'soft-sounding' institutional affiliations could create a negative halo effect, producing bias against researchers at low-status institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such a halo exists, findings may reflect bias against low-status institutions rather than pro-high-status bias; either form undermines objectivity and warrants criticism. Researchers should consider this interpretation and design controls to distinguish halo from prestige-bias effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confounding factor — modifications to original manuscripts must preserve meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentators argued that expository changes to original papers could have altered meaning or readability and thus affected outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure modifications are purely cosmetic and preserve meaning and readability; obtain editors' feedback where possible. Provide empirical/ logical evidence that alterations did not plausibly account for observed variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics of deception — cost–benefit analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Deceptive/unobtrusive methods raise ethical objections; whether deception is justified depends on contextual cost–benefit reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deception may be warranted if (a) there is no feasible alternative way to gather the data, (b) the deception causes no significant physical or psychological harm, and (c) the knowledge gained is potentially of social or economic importance. Researchers should weigh relativist (cost–benefit) and nonconsequentialist objections explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtaining permissions and non-disclosure from authors/publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Twelve of 13 original authors gave permission to disguise manuscripts; publishers were asked not to disclose the study to their editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where deception is used, obtain permission from original authors and publishers where possible; document permissions and procedural safeguards (e.g., not disclosing identities). Report limitations where permission was not obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of journals and articles — limits of citation indices
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentators questioned using citation indices uncritically to establish journal/paper quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on citation counts alone; consider multiple criteria (e.g., author ratings, journal prestige, number of active researchers, journal age, tone of citations). Be transparent about selection criteria and note exclusion of blind-review journals if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size (Small N) considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: A small sample (e.g., 13 journals, analyzable data from 12, 38 editors/reviewers) limits the strength of causal inferences and statistical power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge limitations; provide univariate comparisons and probability calculations appropriate to N; share raw data for future meta-analyses; frame such studies developmentally when resource-constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing randomness (unreliability) from bias explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commentators favor random-error (unreliability) explanations, others bias; the authors argue the two need not be mutually exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both outcome patterns (e.g., proportion of previously published manuscripts rejected) and reviewer agreement statistics to evaluate whether randomness alone explains the data. Apply conditional probability analyses to assess plausibility of pure-randomness models versus models including bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer agreement metrics and interpretation (kappa/intraclass correlation)
rubrics_metrics.description: High levels of reviewer agreement (kappa/Ri values) are rare; reported intraclass correlations of ~.55 are at the high end of the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report chance-adjusted agreement (kappa/Ri), not raw percentages; explain indexing/reindexing differences (e.g., 79% vs 65% precise agreement); compare observed agreement to expected chance agreement and published benchmarks; interpret high agreement cautiously (may reflect agreement on invalid cues like prestige).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical assumptions (chi-square independence and dependence of editors/reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Including editors in chi-square calculations may violate independence assumptions because editors and reviewers are dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recalculate under conservative assumptions to test robustness; justify inclusion/exclusion of dependent units; where independence is dubious, perform sensitivity analyses demonstrating conclusions hold under reasonable alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalisability across disciplines
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commentators argued that observed outcomes might be unique to social sciences, while others thought problems generalize across fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess differences in acceptance/review practices across disciplines (e.g., physics vs psychology acceptance rates) before generalizing; collect cross-disciplinary data where possible rather than assuming universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection rates (editors detecting previously published manuscripts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Low detection rates (many editors did not detect that resubmitted manuscripts had been previously published) are an indicator of weaknesses in reviewer/editor awareness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure detection rates empirically; poll independent editors to estimate expected detection; interpret surprising low detection as evidence warranting further inquiry into review processes and literature familiarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative interpretations to account for rejection rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible alternatives include that selected papers were marginal or ordinary with faults, second reviewer pools differed (e.g., younger/more critical), or methodological flaws were invoked as a universal criticism to mask other reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider and test these alternative hypotheses (e.g., analyze paper quality independently, compare reviewer demographics across review rounds); do not assume a single cause without ruling out plausible alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate reporting and use of literature (avoid selective/misleading citation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics accused selective or misleading use of prior studies; authors defend their reporting as accurate when accounting for chance-adjusted indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When summarizing prior work, use the same metrics (e.g., kappa vs raw agreement) and indexing conventions; be explicit about chance adjustments and indexing; avoid taking statistics out of context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind reviewing as a remedy (pros and cons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many commentators favored blind reviewing as a step to remedy concerns; others noted practical limits (authors reveal identity, editors still know identities) and disciplinary differences in appropriateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider adopting blind review for journals as it reduces reviewer guessing of identity (15–30% accurate guesses observed), but acknowledge limits: editors are not blind and authors can reveal identity; weigh differently for grant reviews where PI identity may be necessary to assess feasibility. Empirical tests of effectiveness are advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial accountability and editors' role in reviewer assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors play a critical role and can influence manuscript disposition by assigning particular reviewers, affecting bias and reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote editorial accountability and responsibility; study editorial assignment procedures; consider reforms that increase transparency and checks on editor influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant reviewing vs journal reviewing — differences in need for identity information
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant proposals function as promises where PI track record and institutional resources matter; blind review may be inappropriate for grant review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For grant review, consider keeping identity information nonblind unless evidence shows institutional/personal bias outweighs the need to assess PI competence. Examine empirical cases (e.g., resubmission with prestigious co-PI altering funding outcome) when deciding policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unobtrusive (deceptive) methods versus participant consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors argue editors/reviewers may change behavior if asked to participate, invoking observational reactivity and experimenter-expectancy effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measuring true behavior of gatekeepers, unobtrusive methods may be necessary to avoid reactivity; when using such methods, carefully justify ethical grounds, seek permissions where possible, and discuss trade-offs between validity and ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish method reliability from trait validity
rubrics_metrics.description: High agreement among reviewers could reflect agreement on invalid components (method effects like prestige) rather than valid trait reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting interrater reliability, consider whether agreement pertains to valid indicators of manuscript quality or to shared biases (e.g., institutional prestige). Use construct-validity checks and multi-method evidence to separate trait from method effects.
